plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two panels side by side to tie the circular and graphical pictures of the sine function together. At the left, drawn faintly in gray, is a unit circle crossed by its axes and by a fan of radii at the special angles. At the right is a Cartesian plot with a horizontal axis labeled x and a vertical axis labeled y ticked at 1, 0, and -1; a solid dark blue curve labeled y = sin(x) enters from the left with an arrowhead, passes through the origin, climbs to a peak of 1, and turns downward toward a second arrowhead. Four dashed orange vertical segments drop from the curve to x-axis ticks labeled pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, and pi/2, and four dashed teal horizontal lines run leftward from those same curve points, across the gap between panels, to matching heights on the gray circle. The teal connectors carry the comparison the figure is built for: the height of a point on the unit circle at a given angle is the value plotted above that angle on the graph. Reading the sine graph as a running record of height on the circle is what lets quadrant position account for the sign of the function.

interactionPlan.concept: The sine value at an angle is the y-coordinate, or vertical height, of the corresponding point on the unit circle, and the sine graph records that height as the angle changes.

demo_steps.title: Start at zero height
demo_steps.narration: At x = 0, the radius points along the positive x-axis, so the circle point has height 0. The matching point on the graph is therefore at the origin.

demo_steps.title: Match a circle height to a graph height
demo_steps.narration: Drag to a special angle such as π/4. The teal horizontal connector shows that the height of the point on the circle is the same value plotted on the sine curve.

demo_steps.title: Reach the maximum
demo_steps.narration: At x = π/2, the radius reaches the top of the unit circle. The y-coordinate is 1, so the sine graph reaches its first peak.

demo_steps.title: Watch the quarter-turn trace the graph
demo_steps.narration: Play the sweep animation to see the radius rotate from 0 to π/2 while the sine curve is traced from the origin to its maximum. The graph is a running record of vertical height on the circle.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A point on the sine graph is not separate from the unit circle: it is the unit-circle point's vertical coordinate plotted against the angle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a side-by-side layout with the unit circle on the left and the sine graph on the right. Keep the original visual hierarchy: pale gray circle and radii, dark blue sine curve, orange dashed vertical angle markers, and teal dashed horizontal height connectors. The current interactive angle should be emphasized with a darker rotating radius, a marked point on the circle, a marked point on the curve, one orange vertical drop to the x-axis, and one teal horizontal connector spanning from the graph point back to the same height on the circle. The sine curve should rise from the origin to y = 1 at π/2 and then bend slightly downward to the right, matching the source figure's visible continuation.

authoredContext:
Notice how the sine values are positive between 0 and π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants I and II on the unit circle, and the sine values are negative between π and 2π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants III and IV on the unit circle. See the figure.

Plotting values of the sine function

A side-by-side graph of a unit circle and a graph of sin(x). The two graphs show the equivalence of the coordinates.

Increase the pi-fraction tick label size slightly and position them closer to the source layout for better inline readability.
Avoid drawing the teal dynamic connector along the x-axis in the default state, since it visually reads as an extra dashed construction line not present in the source.
